title: Not Ashamed: Fan the Gift into Flame
summary: Writing from prison, Paul thanks God for Timothy, remembering his tears and the sincere faith first held by his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. He urges Timothy to rekindle the gift of God, not to be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul the prisoner, and to share in suffering, because God has saved and called us by his grace in Christ Jesus, who abolished death. Paul contrasts those in Asia who deserted him with Onesiphorus, who searched Rome to find him and was not ashamed of his chains.
story: When 1 Timothy was written, Paul was free and traveling. Now he is a prisoner, and the tone has changed. This chapter opens what many readers take to be Paul's last letter, and its first concern is courage. Timothy may have been tempted to keep his distance from a condemned man, or to lose heart as false teaching spread and friends fell away. Paul answers with memory (Timothy's own faith, his family, his commissioning), with doctrine (the grace given in Christ before time began), and with examples, bad and good. The key word of the chapter is shame: Paul is not ashamed, Timothy must not be, and Onesiphorus was not.
historical:
Paul is in chains (verse 16) in Rome (verse 17). If, as early tradition holds, he was released from the house arrest described in Acts 28 and later rearrested, this imprisonment would fall in the mid-60s AD, under the emperor Nero. After the great fire of Rome in AD 64, according to the historian Tacitus, Nero blamed the Christians and had many of them executed. Visiting or supporting a Christian prisoner in that climate carried real risk. Onesiphorus had to search diligently to find Paul, which suggests a harsher confinement than the rented quarters of Acts 28:30.

The Province of Asia (verse 15) was the Roman province in the west of what is now Turkey, with Ephesus as its leading city. Paul had spent years there, and the churches of the region were among the fruits of his work (Acts 19:10). That everyone in Asia had deserted him probably means that believers from Asia who might have supported him in Rome, or at his trial, turned away; it need not mean every Christian in the province abandoned the faith. Phygelus and Hermogenes are otherwise unknown. Scholars who see the letter as written by a later follower of Paul read these details as part of a farewell testament; those who hold that Paul wrote it see them as the natural detail of a real situation.
cultural:
Timothy's faith came through his mother's side. Acts 16:1 says his mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek, and here Paul names his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. In a Jewish home the Scriptures were taught to children from an early age (3:15), and Timothy's faith in Christ grew out of that inheritance. Paul also speaks of serving God as his forefathers did (verse 3). He did not think of his faith in Christ as a break from Israel's God but as its fulfillment.

Shame and honor were powerful forces in the Roman world. Imprisonment was a public disgrace, and a prisoner's friends shared that dishonor if they stood by him. Prisoners often depended on friends and family for food, clothing, and other needs, since the authorities provided little. Onesiphorus refreshing Paul (verse 16) probably meant practical help as well as friendship. The laying on of hands (verse 6) was an act of commissioning, and Paul's reference to his own hands, alongside the elders' hands in 1 Timothy 4:14, recalls the moment Timothy was set apart for ministry.
literary: The chapter begins with the customary letter opening and thanksgiving (verses 1-5), warm with personal memory: tears, prayer night and day, longing, joy. Verses 6-14 form the main appeal, a series of commands (fan into flame, do not be ashamed, join in suffering, hold on, guard) built around one of the letter's great summaries of the gospel (verses 9-10), which may draw on early Christian confession. Verses 15-18 close with contrasting examples. The chapter is held together by the language of shame (verses 8, 12, and 16) and of guarding what is entrusted (verses 12 and 14). The phrase “that day” (verses 12 and 18) points to the day of Christ's return and judgment, which frames everything Paul endures.

outline.t: Greeting to Timothy, a beloved child
Fan into flame the gift of God
Do not be ashamed: the grace revealed in Christ Jesus
Hold the pattern and guard the treasure
Deserters in Asia and the faithful Onesiphorus

doctrines.note: God “has saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began” (verse 9). Salvation starts in God's eternal purpose and is received as grace, not earned.

God has not given a spirit of fear but “of power, love, and self-control” (verse 7), and the Holy Spirit who dwells in believers helps them guard the gospel (verse 14). Courage in ministry is a gift, not a personality trait.
Suffering for the gospel is shared (“join me in suffering”) and is borne “by the power of God” (verse 8). Paul's confidence in suffering rests not on his own strength but on the one he has believed.
Christ Jesus “has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel” (verse 10). The coming day of the Lord (verses 12 and 18) is the horizon of faithful endurance.

words.note: Anazōpureō, to rekindle or stir up into flame, found only here in the New Testament. The image is of coals that need fanning to burn brightly. It does not necessarily imply that Timothy's gift had gone out, but that gifts need tending and can grow dim with neglect or fear.

Deilia, timidity or cowardice, found only here in the New Testament. The Spirit God gives is not one of fearful shrinking back, but of power, love, and self-control. The word suggests that fear, not lack of ability, was the danger Timothy faced.

Epaischunomai, to be ashamed of. It appears three times in the chapter (verses 8, 12, and 16) and is the key word of the chapter. Jesus warned that whoever is ashamed of him and his words, he will be ashamed of when he comes (Mark 8:38), and Paul had written that he was not ashamed of the gospel (Romans 1:16).

Parathēkē, a deposit held in trust. Verse 12 can be read as what Paul has entrusted to God (his life and ministry) or what God has entrusted to Paul (the gospel); verse 14 clearly means the gospel entrusted to Timothy. Either way, God and his servants are bound by a trust that God will keep.

christ: Verses 9-10 compress the whole story of salvation into a few lines centered on Christ Jesus. Grace was given in him before time began, so that God's saving purpose was always a purpose in Christ. That grace has now been revealed through his appearing, meaning his coming into the world. He has abolished death, not by removing it from human experience, but by breaking its power, and he has brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. Paul's confidence in prison rests here: “I know whom I have believed” (verse 12). The object of faith is not a doctrine alone but a person, able to guard what has been entrusted until that day. The faith and love that Timothy is to hold are “in Christ Jesus” (verse 13).

hard.q: Was Onesiphorus dead, and is Paul praying for the dead?
hard.a:
Paul prays for mercy for the household of Onesiphorus (verse 16) and for Onesiphorus himself on that day (verse 18), and later greets his household but not him (4:19). Many interpreters conclude that Onesiphorus had died, perhaps as a result of his visit to Rome. Roman Catholic and Orthodox interpreters have often read verse 18 as a prayer for a departed believer and as support for the practice of praying for the dead, which also has a precedent in 2 Maccabees 12:43-45, a book in their Old Testament.

Many Protestant interpreters answer that the text does not say Onesiphorus had died; he may simply have been away from home, which would explain why his household is greeted separately. They add that even if he had died, a brief wish that the Lord show him mercy at the judgment is different from a developed practice of prayer on behalf of the dead. The verse is short and its circumstances unknown, and it has been read differently across Christian traditions. What is clear is Paul's gratitude for a friend who was not ashamed of him.

questions: Paul traces Timothy's faith through his grandmother and mother. Who handed faith to you, and to whom are you handing it?
Where are you tempted to be ashamed of the gospel, or of people associated with it, and what would courage look like there?
Paul says God gave a spirit of power, love, and self-control rather than fear. Which of those three do you most need, and why?
